Basal metabolic rate in the Lyre-tailed nightjar was measured using flow-through respirometry on post-absorptive, inactive individuals during their nocturnal rest phase, yielding a mean oxygen consumption of 94.55 milliliters per hour [JOi = 94.55 milliliters per hour] at a body temperature of 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C], which represents the maximum resting metabolic rate for this species. While this value is somewhat elevated relative to predictions based on body mass alone among Caprimulgidae, it likely reflects the high energetic demands of the species' hovering display flights and the cost of maintaining the remarkably elongated outer rectrices that characterize adult males. Field-collected data on reproductive output indicate that females produce two eggs per clutch, a clutch size that is typical for the family, and they generally raise a single clutch each year. This low annual fecundity is consistent with a life-history strategy oriented toward adult survival in a relatively stable, albeit resource-limited, montane environment. The extraordinarily long tail feathers, which can exceed the body length in males, likely impose additional aerodynamic and energetic costs during the breeding season, possibly constraining the number of broods a female can successfully fledge within a single year.

Eggs of the Lyre-tailed nightjar are incubated for approximately 19.5 days [ab = approximately 19.5 days] when maintained at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a duration that is consistent with the typical incubation period observed across the Caprimulgidae. Upon hatching, the altricial nestlings weigh roughly 6.1 grams [Wwb = roughly 6.1 grams], representing a modest initial body mass that reflects the relatively small egg size characteristic of this family. This neonatal mass is notably low when compared to the asymptotic adult body mass attained by females, which reaches approximately 77.5 grams [Wwi = approximately 77.5 grams], indicating a substantial degree of postnatal growth. The developmental trajectory from hatching to nutritional independence is relatively rapid among nightjars, with fledging occurring at 20 days after hatching [tx = 20 days after hatching] when maintained at 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C], a period during which the growing chick undergoes a remarkable transformation in both size and plumage development.

The onset of puberty in the Lyre-tailed nightjar is reached at 60 days after hatching [tp = 60 days after hatching] when individuals are maintained at a body temperature of 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C], marking the point at which gonadal development reaches maturity and the individual becomes physiologically capable of reproduction. This relatively rapid attainment of sexual maturity, compared to other caprimulgids of similar body size, may be an adaptation to the short breeding season characteristic of its high-altitude Andean habitat, where favorable conditions for rearing young are temporally constrained. Field observations further indicate that the first successful reproductive event typically occurs at approximately 511 days after hatching [tR = approximately 511 days after hatching] when ambient temperatures reach 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], suggesting that while physiological maturity is achieved early, ecological or social factors may delay actual breeding until the second year of life. This delayed first reproduction, combined with the single annual clutch, underscores a conservative life-history strategy that prioritizes adult survival and prolonged reproductive lifespan over high immediate reproductive output.

The maximum recorded lifespan for the Lyre-tailed nightjar has been estimated at approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years] under natural field conditions, with the highest longevity observations made at 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C], a value that places this species among the longer-lived members of the Caprimulgidae. This relatively extended lifespan, when considered alongside the modest clutch size and delayed first reproduction, is characteristic of a slow life-history pace that is often associated with species inhabiting stable, resource-limited environments such as the montane cloud forests of the northern Andes. Adult survival rates are presumably high, supported by a cryptic plumage that provides effective camouflage against predators and a nocturnal foraging strategy that reduces competition with diurnal insectivores. The combination of a 10-year maximum lifespan (10 years) [am = 10 years], a low annual reproductive output, and a deferred age at first reproduction reflects an evolved trade-off whereby the species invests heavily in self-maintenance and longevity at the expense of high fecundity, a pattern observed in many tropical and subtropical bird lineages at a temperature of 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C].

Comparative studies among Andean caprimulgids reveal that the Lyre-tailed nightjar exhibits a basal metabolic rate that is somewhat elevated relative to allometric predictions based on its body mass, a finding that may be linked to the energetic demands of its elaborate sexual ornamentation. The remarkably elongated outer rectrices of males, which can exceed the body length, likely impose significant aerodynamic costs during flight, requiring greater pectoral muscle mass and hence higher resting metabolic expenditure. In terms of reproductive ecology, the species' preference for rocky outcrops and steep slopes in montane forest underscores its dependence on specific microhabitats for nesting, which may limit population density and gene flow among isolated populations. Future research should focus on quantifying the energetic costs of tail ornamentation through controlled flight experiments and examining the relationship between individual variation in metabolic rate and reproductive success, as these factors are likely to be crucial for understanding the evolutionary dynamics shaping the life history of this remarkable bird.
